# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum stood between a locksmith and a shop that sold only blue objects. Nobody could remember what had occupied the building before it became a museum, although the locksmith insisted it had once been a narrower building. From the street, it appeared to have three floors. From the staircase, it had seven, provided you did not count the landing where it was always raining.

Admission was free. The opening hours were written on a brass plate:

**TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY  
WHENEVER YOU ARE READY**

On Mondays, the museum was closed for dusting and regret.

Mara had worked there for twenty-three years. Her official title was Keeper of Incomplete Acquisitions, though she was also the ticket attendant, archivist, electrician, and person responsible for explaining why visitors could not finish the crossword in Gallery Four.

“But I know seventeen across,” they would say.

“That isn’t the point,” Mara would reply.

Occasionally, someone would fill it in when her back was turned. By morning, the letters were gone. The pencil, however, would have become slightly shorter.

This was one of the museum’s gentler defenses.

***

The collection had begun with a sweater.

It was green, or had intended to be green before its maker changed yarn halfway through the chest. One sleeve was complete. The other ended just below the shoulder in a fringe of loose wool. It arrived folded in a paper bag, accompanied by a note:

*My mother was making this for my father. Then she decided to leave him. Neither event explains the other as much as you might think.*

There was no signature.

Mara displayed the sweater on a wooden chair rather than a mannequin. She thought it looked less accused that way.

Other things followed.

A chess game abandoned in 1964, with black in an apparently winning position. A doctoral thesis on the sleeping habits of bees. The foundations of a house, somehow delivered in a shoebox. Three bars of a melody that made everyone who heard it turn toward the nearest window.

There were unfinished meals, unfinished migrations, and one unfinished Tuesday.

The Tuesday required refrigeration.

Mara liked practical objects best. A chair without a seat made no attempt to disguise its situation. A half-carved spoon was pleasantly specific about what had happened to it. Letters were more difficult. They often believed they were finished, especially the cruel ones.

The museum had a room full of letters that ended, *And another thing—*

Visitors rarely stayed there long.

***

Every acquisition received a label.

**OBJECT 114: WOODEN BOAT**  
**Maker unknown**  
**Abandoned before the mast was fitted**

At first, Mara had written longer descriptions. She had speculated about interruption, poverty, illness, distraction. She had used phrases such as *the pressures of ordinary life* and *a testament to thwarted ambition.*

Then a carpenter visited the museum and studied a cabinet whose drawers had never been installed.

“Could just be he got sick of cabinets,” the carpenter said.

After that, Mara restricted herself to facts.

Even facts could be troublesome. The boat, for example, had been donated by a woman who said her husband died before he could finish it. Six months later, the husband appeared, very much alive, and asked for it back.

“She tells people that when she’s angry,” he explained.

Mara returned the boat. Two weeks afterward, it arrived again, now with a mast but no sail.

This time the note said:

*He has taken up pottery.*

***

The boy came on a wet Thursday in November.

He was perhaps twelve, with a serious face and a schoolbag that appeared to contain bricks. He stood just inside the entrance until Mara looked up from repairing a label.

“Is this where you keep things people didn’t finish?”

“Some of them.”

“Who decides which ones?”

“Usually the stairs.”

He considered this without smiling.

“I’ve brought something.”

He took a small black recorder from his bag and placed it on the desk. It was the sort journalists once carried, with physical buttons and a wrist strap. A strip of masking tape on the back read **DAD**.

Mara did not touch it.

“Would you like to tell me about it?”

“My father used to record things. Birds. Trains. Our refrigerator when it was making a noise. He said machines were easier to understand if you listened before you opened them.”

The boy pressed play.

There was a click, a breath, and the distant scrape of a chair.

Then a man’s voice said, “Eli, there’s something I should have told you before—”

The recording stopped.

Outside, a bus sighed at the curb.

“Is there more on the tape?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Do you know what interrupted him?”

“He turned it off.”

***

Mara had learned not to ask certain questions too quickly.

She offered the boy a chair. He remained standing.

“He died in February,” he said. “Not while recording it. Later.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Everyone is.”

He looked around the entrance hall, where an unfinished portrait seemed to be listening with its one completed ear.

“Can you find out the rest?”

“No,” Mara said.

The speed of her answer surprised him.

“You haven’t tried.”

“I know what the museum can do.”

“What can it do?”

“Keep it safe. Give you somewhere to leave it.”

“I have a drawer.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “You do.”

The boy put the recorder back in his bag.

She expected him to leave, but he looked at the staircase.

“What’s upstairs?”

“Things people thought they would come back to.”

“Did they?”

“Some.”

He shifted the bag onto both shoulders.

“I’ll look.”

***

He returned the next Thursday, and the Thursday after that.

His name was Eli. He disliked being asked how school was. He liked the refrigerated Tuesday, particularly the sandwich suspended halfway between a plate and an absent mouth. He spent a long time with a model railway whose tracks stopped at the edge of a meticulously painted village.

“Why didn’t they make the rest?”

“Space, perhaps.”

“They could have made a smaller village.”

“Perhaps they liked the village.”

He bent until his face was level with the tiny station.

“There’s nobody waiting.”

“No.”

“That’s good.”

By December, Mara had begun keeping biscuits in the desk. She pretended they were for everyone, although the museum’s other regular visitor, a retired surveyor, could not eat wheat.

Eli noticed.

“You could buy him something else.”

So she did.

The surveyor accepted his almond biscuit with solemn gratitude and then asked, for the ninth time, whether the unfinished map on the top floor represented an actual place.

Mara gave her usual answer.

“Not yet.”

***

The map was hers.

She had drawn it at nineteen, when she and her sister planned to cross the country on bicycles. It showed back roads, cheap campsites, public fountains, and a town where someone reportedly sold the best peaches in the world.

Their route ended at the sea.

Three weeks before departure, their father fell down the cellar stairs and broke his hip. Their mother had been dead for years. Mara stayed to help. Her sister, Lena, went alone.

That was the simple account.

The less simple account contained a quarrel beside a kitchen sink, six months of unanswered letters, a postcard Mara tore in half, and a sentence spoken with such precision that she could still remember the shape of her sister’s mouth afterward.

She had brought the map to the museum during her first week of employment.

The previous keeper hung it without asking questions.

Mara had been grateful to him.

She had never considered whether gratitude was the right response.

***

One afternoon, Eli found her on the top floor replacing a lightbulb.

“Did you make that?”

He pointed to the map.

“Yes.”

“Why did you stop?”

“Family trouble.”

“Did the trouble stop?”

Mara tightened the bulb a little too firmly.

“Eventually.”

“Then why didn’t you go?”

She climbed down from the stepladder.

“By then, other things had happened.”

“What things?”

“A job. Responsibilities.”

He waited.

“I got older,” she said.

“My teacher cycled to France. She’s sixty.”

“Your teacher sounds energetic.”

Eli examined the map again.

“You drew a ferry.”

“Yes.”

“There isn’t any sea.”

“I hadn’t got that far.”

He traced the route without touching the paper.

“So you finished the journey before you finished the map.”

Mara opened her mouth, then closed it.

The bulb above them gave a small, satisfied click.

***

In January, the museum began misbehaving.

This was distinct from its normal behavior.

The incomplete Tuesday developed a Wednesday along one edge. The green sweater grew three stitches overnight. In Gallery Four, seventeen across filled itself in.

The answer was **MERCY**.

Mara checked the security cameras. They showed nothing except the retired surveyor standing very still before the map, eating an almond biscuit from his coat pocket.

Then the wooden boat returned.

It appeared on the entrance desk on a Monday morning, though the doors had been locked. There was still no sail. Instead, its maker had fitted a small electric motor.

Attached was a note:

*Apparently this counts.*

Mara was still reading it when someone knocked.

A woman stood outside carrying a canvas toolbox.

“Building inspection,” she said.

“We had one last spring.”

“You had a fire inspection. I’m here about the other problem.”

“What other problem?”

The woman looked up.

A fourth-floor window had appeared above the third.

“Your premises are becoming definite.”

***

The inspector’s name was Mrs. Vale. She wore muddy boots and carried a measuring tape that occasionally measured things before she asked it to.

She examined the sweater, the crossword, and the refrigerated Tuesday.

Then she sat at Mara’s desk.

“How many objects have been reclaimed in the past year?”

“Seven.”

“How many acquired?”

“Four hundred and twelve.”

Mrs. Vale wrote something down.

“Do you conduct reviews?”

“Of what?”

“The objects. Their circumstances. Whether they still belong here.”

“They’re unfinished.”

“Yes. When did you last check?”

Mara looked toward the galleries.

Mrs. Vale set down her pen.

“A place like this can hold things while people decide what to do with them. It can hold them for a very long time. But you have several thousand objects here, and hardly anyone seems to know they’re allowed to take them home.”

“It says so on the donation form.”

“Where?”

Mara fetched a form.

The sentence was on the reverse, beneath the insurance exclusions.

***

That evening, Mara stayed late.

She opened the acquisition ledger and began reading.

The thesis on bees belonged to a woman who had become a successful baker. The abandoned chess game had been interrupted by the players deciding to marry. The half-carved spoon was one of eighty-seven attempts made by an apprentice who had subsequently become a master.

Mara had all this information. She had recorded it herself.

Yet the labels said only *unfinished.*

She went upstairs to the map.

The route remained exactly as she had drawn it: hopeful, economical, avoiding steep hills.

In the margin, Lena had sketched a fish wearing a crown.

Mara had forgotten that.

She stood there until the automatic lights went out, then waved one hand to bring them back.

***

Eli arrived the next day to find the entrance hall crowded with empty boxes.

“Are you closing?”

“I’m reviewing the collection.”

“Did someone complain?”

“Yes.”

“Who?”

“The building, apparently.”

He helped her sort correspondence. Together they wrote to makers, donors, descendants. Some addresses no longer existed. Some names had changed. One letter came back with the handwritten explanation, *Gone sailing. Try in June.*

A woman collected an unfinished wedding dress.

“Are you going to finish it?” Eli asked.

“No. I want the silk.”

A man reclaimed a half-written novel and read the first page while standing at the desk.

“Oh, good lord,” he said.

“Would you like some privacy?” Mara asked.

“I’d like a recycling bin.”

She showed him where it was.

For the first time in years, the museum’s windows opened.

He nodded.

Eli turned the recorder over.

“Yes.”

“I hate that.”

“I know.”

This time, after it stopped, he did not immediately rewind it.

Instead, he opened a side pocket of his bag and took out a second tape.

She had found the number through a cousin, which required a conversation she had been avoiding for almost as long as the call itself.

Lena answered on the fifth ring.

“Hello?”

“It’s me,” she said.

“I know.”

For a moment, neither sister spoke.

Then Mara said, “Do you remember the fish you drew on our map?”

“The king of the herrings.”

“Was that what it was?”

“Obviously.”

Mara laughed. The sound startled her.

“I still have it.”

“The fish?”

“The map.”

The chopping stopped.

“Oh,” Lena said.

“I’m sorry,” Mara said.

There was a long pause.

“About which part?”

It was a fair question. Mara sat down.

They spoke for forty minutes. Some of it went badly.

Before hanging up, Lena gave Mara her address.

***

By summer, the museum had become smaller.

The rainy landing disappeared, leaving behind a damp umbrella nobody recognized. Gallery Six became a cupboard. Gallery Seven returned a pair of spectacles Mara had lost eleven years earlier and then ceased to exist.

There were still plenty of exhibits.

Some things needed keeping.

The three bars of music remained, as did the house foundations and several letters whose owners were not ready to touch them. Mara changed the labels where she could.

**Set aside.**

**No longer needed.**

**Awaiting a decision.**

The crossword stayed unfinished. Visitors still complained.

Eli came less often once school ended. On his last visit before a holiday, he brought Mara a recording of the museum: footsteps, the clock, a drawer sticking, rain against the front window.

Near the end, Mara could hear herself asking whether he wanted a biscuit.

Then came his answer, perfectly clear.

She kept the tape in her desk.

On Sunday evening, she took down the map. Her train ticket was tucked into its fold, beside the crowned fish.

At the door, she paused to straighten the opening-hours plaque.

The locksmith was closing up next door.

“Off somewhere?”

“To see my sister.”

“Far?”

“A fair way.”

He offered to check the building while she was gone.

“Just the windows,” Mara said.

“What about the rest?”

She looked back at the museum. Upstairs, a light went out.

“The rest can wait.”
